competitor_mentions.quote: We've started looking more closely at alternatives, Storsund BI among them, partly prompted by moments like this one.
it's part of why Storsund BI keeps coming up in our internal conversations about next year's tooling
we're continuing to look at Storsund BI as part of our renewal planning

narrative: Sparse but escalating pattern of small platform inconsistencies (dashboard share links, an export stuck in queue, a report template reset) that the account routinely fixes manually rather than trusting the platform's own repair, e.g. 'we've since renewed them manually as a stopgap.' Storsund BI is explicitly named in three consecutive tickets with rising seriousness, culminating in 'we're continuing to look at Storsund BI as part of our renewal planning.' No anger anywhere in the text, but a quiet accumulation of distrust — the classic slow-churn signature.

A single silent-failure defect (cached or stale data served with no error) recurs across connectors, API, and report builder from December through April, most visibly when the exact same stale-template symptom hit twice in two weeks: 'happened again — same report, same stale-template symptom as the one from a couple of weeks ago.' The customer has stopped trusting the fix cycle and now runs a manual pre-send checklist 'on every scheduled send as standard practice' — a workaround hardening into permanence even though the tone stays calm and non-confrontational.

Five well-spaced, routine tickets over seven months covering a connector outage, a stale dashboard, an alert-setup how-to, a template-merge question, and a missed export. Resolution times run six to twelve days but the customer never complains about pace and no issue is re-raised, indicating ordinary usage rather than building dissatisfaction.

competitor_mentions.quote: we evaluated Dashlume earlier in the year but stuck with Kataja because the reporting depth won out — good to confirm that decision was right

narrative: Consistently positive, engaged account — compliments on report builder flexibility ('really pleased with how flexible the builder has been') and the new dashboard layout, feature requests rather than complaints, and an explicit reaffirmation that Kataja beat Dashlume in an earlier evaluation. No unresolved threads and no friction; a reference-account profile.

Only two tickets on record. The most recent (alert threshold resetting on every edit) is still open and mildly annoying — 'having to re-enter it each time, which is a bit error-prone' — but not urgent. Too little history to call a real trend; worth a light watch rather than treating as a risk case.

Sustained breakdown across nearly every module from October 2024 to February 2025: batch exports drop rows silently, alert emails stop entirely ('we're effectively blind'), large exports time out, and a prior connector fix is explicitly called out as never having worked — 'I had a similar issue flagged months ago and was told it was resolved. It clearly wasn't. I need this escalated.' Four separate issue threads remain open with no resolution by the end of the record, and tone has shifted from technical detail to open demands for accountability.
Two simple, well-spaced requests (currency formatting, adding a user) both closed quickly with no complaint. No signal of risk in either the volume or the tone.

Four routine tickets over nine months — alert distribution, a new connector request, alert frequency tuning, a locked template — each resolved without recurrence or complaint. A healthy, low-touch account.

Frequent but mostly minor traffic across a year. One genuine open defect — report builder silently failing to save reports with more than three charts, 'happened twice this week' — has no confirmed fix anywhere in the record. Later tickets, including a routine pre-renewal seat-count check, read as business-as-usual rather than dissatisfaction.

An Enterprise regional account where four sparse, polite tickets build a case file: a distribution-list update that wouldn't persist, report builder slowness serious enough that 'a couple of the regional finance leads have gone back to compiling their sections in Excel,' and recurring regional connector sync failures that prompted permanent local export fallbacks — 'operationally we're covered either way. Wanted this on record for our upcoming renewal conversation.' No named competitor, but the explicit renewal framing plus quietly-adopted workarounds mirror the slow-churn pattern seen elsewhere in the book.

Three unrelated one-off technical issues (token expiry, CSV encoding of Nordic characters, connector auth after an ERP upgrade) each resolved within a week, with no recurrence or complaint. Normal operational traffic.

Six tickets over a year mixing minor bugs and feature requests — export limits, date formatting, row grouping, a new HubSpot connector — all resolved without repeat complaints. Healthy engagement, including active interest in expanding the connector set.

competitor_mentions.quote: it's exactly the kind of thing that's come up as we've started comparing notes with Storsund BI ahead of renewal discussions
particularly with Storsund BI's alerting being one of the things under comparison
Storsund BI has moved from a background comparison to something we're actively evaluating properly for next year

narrative: Starts routine (a dashboard feature request, a seat-count credit) but from May 2025 the account explicitly threads together API auth errors, a non-firing alert, and dashboard timestamp mismatches as 'the run of small things this year,' with Storsund BI escalating from a passing comparison to 'something we're actively evaluating properly for next year.' The final ticket is deliberately filed as 'no need to treat this one urgently' — minimising language layered on top of an active competitive evaluation, a high-risk combination despite the consistently calm tone.

Mostly simple configuration requests. One bug — alerts firing outside business hours — recurs on a second alert eight months later ('similar to the alert scheduling issue from earlier in the year'), suggesting the root cause was never fully fixed, though the customer's tone stays matter-of-fact rather than frustrated.

competitor_mentions.quote: We are also, separately, looking at Dashlume as part of a broader vendor review this year, and ease of credential management is one of the criteria on the list.
this is exactly the kind of thing coming up in our Dashlume comparison, for what it's worth

narrative: A short but fast-building account: a normal feature question in January is followed by an urgent API credential failure blocking a partner deadline, explicitly raised during 'a broader vendor review' that includes Dashlume, then a minor alert misconfiguration is folded into the same comparison — 'the accumulation of small admin-side issues this year... is exactly the kind of thing coming up in our Dashlume comparison.' Short history, but a clear and recent serious competitive threat.

Five varied one-off requests and bugs (webhook alert, dashboard embedding, cross-connector reporting, SSO login, a chart missing on export) each resolved within days with no recurrence or complaint. Ordinary usage pattern.

Sparse account with one open but explicitly low-priority item — a stuck export flagged only 'so it doesn't just sit there,' the customer already having sourced the data elsewhere — and two otherwise routine tickets. No urgency or dissatisfaction anywhere in the text.

A grinding 2024 arc: an unresolved user-deactivation bug from May is still open when API latency worsens in July ('I'm starting to wonder if these are getting proper attention'), and by August three separate issues are open at once — 'I need someone to actually look at our account and tell me what's going on.' Even after the September outage and October dashboard staleness were fixed, the November export ticket is filed with open skepticism, 'the fix we were offered didn't hold,' leaving three threads genuinely unresolved and trust badly damaged.

A rough 2024 (three modules broke in succession, with 15-16 day fixes) recurs in a May 2025 crisis where the customer demands 'someone senior to own this' after simultaneous API and connector outages. The account then pivots decisively: direct phone contact resolves the dashboard fallout with explicit thanks — 'that kind of communication would have helped a lot earlier in the year too' — and the two follow-up tickets are calm to positive, including a proactive question about failure notifications. A textbook anger-to-resolution arc; the dramatic history matters less than the genuinely rebuilt trust visible in the last two tickets.

Light early-lifecycle traffic — connector setup help, a low-priority own-email-change bug still open but explicitly 'not urgent,' and a first-alert setup question. No complaint pattern or urgency; reads as a normal onboarding-stage account.
